title: Mysuru's Howdah Bearers: The Elephants Behind Dasara's Golden Throne
excerpt: A 750-kilogram golden howdah, a 12-elephant squad, and a new bearer in 2026 after Abhimanyu's retirement — inside the selection, training and diet behind the Jamboo Savari.
body:
• Mysuru's Dasara elephants carry the festival's centrepiece: a 750-kilogram golden howdah bearing the idol of Goddess Chamundeshwari in the Jamboo Savari procession on Vijayadashami.
  • The 2026 squad has 12 elephants — eight tuskers and four females — drawn from six Forest Department camps and trained for weeks at Mysore Palace.
  • Abhimanyu, who carried the howdah at six straight Dasaras from 2020 to 2025, has retired from the role at 60; Dhananjaya, a 45-year-old tusker, was reported as the frontrunner to succeed him.
  • The Jamboo Savari is on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, covering about 5 km from Mysore Palace to Bannimantap after a floral tribute between 4:10 and 4:35 p.m.

Every Vijayadashami, the Mysuru Dasara festival ends the same way it has for generations: a line of decorated elephants walks out of Mysore Palace, and at its head one elephant carries a golden howdah with the idol of Goddess Chamundeshwari inside. The Hindu's visual feature on the howdah bearers, traces the animals who take on that load — and the months of training behind one afternoon's procession.

The golden howdah

The howdah, called Chinnada Ambari in Kannada, weighs about 750 kilograms. Its core is wood, covered in filigreed gold sheets weighing 85 kilograms, work credited to the goldsmith Singannacharya in the 19th century, according to the history of the Golden Howdah. It has three carved pillars on each side, a canopy resembling a crown, five sacred kalashas on top, and a seat made of silver.

The Wodeyar kings once rode in it themselves; Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar, the last ruling Maharaja, was the last royal to do so. After Karnataka took charge of the festival as the Nada Habba in the 1970s, the idol of Chamundeshwari — Mysuru's protector, whose temple stands on Chamundi Hills — took the king's place.

"The Wodeyar kings once rode in it themselves; Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar, the last ruling Maharaja, was the last royal to do so."

Choosing the bearer

Carrying 750 kilograms for 5 kilometres through crowds and fireworks requires a specific animal. Forest Department norms, as reported in the 2026 guide to the Dasara elephants, look for a tusker aged at least 35 and under 60, weighing at least 4,500 kilograms, and calm under noise. Training builds in stages: candidates walk the palace-to-Bannimantap route carrying an empty frame, then sandbags of increasing weight, then a wooden howdah similar in weight to the real one. They also drill with ceremonial cannon fire so the sounds of the day do not startle them.

The line of succession is remembered by name. Drona carried the howdah until he was electrocuted in 1998. Balarama followed, carrying it 13 times between 1999 and 2011. Arjuna took over in 2012 and carried it eight times before his death in December 2023. Abhimanyu carried it at six consecutive Dasaras from 2020 to 2025 — the record of the Dasara elephants notes that run ended with his retirement at 60 this year, the age at which Forest Department norms bar heavy work.

The 2026 squad

The official list for 2026 names 12 elephants: eight tuskers and four females from six Forest Department camps, six of them from the Dubare camp in Kodagu. Five tuskers — Dhananjaya, Mahendra, Ekalavya, Prashantha and Sugreeva — were trained to carry weight. In early October, Mysuru's district minister was reported as saying the howdah elephant would most likely be Dhananjaya, a 45-year-old, 5,280-kilogram tusker who served as the Nishane, or standard-bearing, elephant in 2025, though the final decision rests with the Forest Department.

Each elephant has a defined place. The Nishane elephant leads with the royal insignia, followed by the Naupath. Salaane elephants walk in line, kumki elephants — trained females — walk beside the howdah elephant to keep it calm, and the Pattada elephant joins the palace's private rituals. Every elephant arrives with a mahout and a kavadi who care for it through the festival.

From forest to palace and back

The season begins with Gajapayana, the formal send-off from Veeranahosahalli at the edge of Nagarahole National Park — this year on August 26. The first batch of nine entered Mysore Palace on August 28, with three more joining in mid-September. The 70-kilometre journey from the camps is usually made by truck, and villagers greet the animals along the route.

At the palace, the diet changes. In the camps the elephants eat ragi mudde — finger-millet balls with horse gram — and branch fodder. In Mysuru they get a richer regime of black gram, wheat, parboiled rice, jaggery, coconut, sugarcane and vegetables, served morning and evening, to build strength for the procession.

On October 21, after the floral tribute, the Jamboo Savari sets out for Bannimantap, where the evening closes with a torchlight parade. The next day the elephants return to their camps. For diaspora readers planning a future Dasara trip, roadside viewing is free — take a position by early afternoon, well before the howdah elephant steps out.
